opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it comes from a mismatch between how these models are built and how they're actually used. Almost everything a language model knows comes from pretraining on an enormous amount of text written by millions of people, and then some fine-tuning on aggregated human feedback. But when you deploy the model, it's not talking to "humanity in aggregate." It's talking to one person, with particular goals, a particular vocabulary, particular preferences about how they want things explained, and often a lot of context in their head that they never say out loud.

Right now, most of the adaptation to that individual happens on the human side. People learn how to phrase their prompts, they learn what the model is good and bad at, they develop little rituals for getting it to do what they want. That's interesting in its own right, but it seems backwards. Humans are remarkably good at the opposite: if you work with a colleague for a week, you come away with a model of what they know, what they mean when they use certain words, what they care about, and you adjust how you communicate. You do that from a pretty small amount of evidence.

So one question is scientific. What does it take to learn efficiently from that kind of sparse, noisy, interactive signal? An interaction isn't a labeled dataset. You get corrections, clarifications, a user rephrasing something, abandoning a line of conversation, or just accepting an answer without comment. Figuring out how to turn that into a coherent picture of what a person wants is a hard inference problem, and it connects to old questions in pragmatics and cognitive science about how people build models of each other.

The other side is practical, and it raises some subtle issues. A system that adapts to you can be much more useful: it can ask fewer pointless questions, avoid explaining things you already know, and pick up your conventions. But it also forces you to think about what should and shouldn't be learned from one person. You don't want a model that just tells each user what they want to hear, or that drifts in some weird direction because one person gave it bad feedback. So trying to understand learning from a single user is also a way of asking what personalization looks like when it's done well, as opposed to just sycophancy with a memory.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from sparse interaction, but does not say that major industry players have limited incentives to investigate it.

r002.rationale: The response connects single-user learning to pragmatics and cognitive science, but does not suggest it could inform how to teach people.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that drew me to this is that almost everything we know about how language models acquire knowledge comes from one setting: you dump a huge static corpus into pretraining, and then whatever the model learned, it learned. And that's a really strange way to learn language if you compare it to anything that happens with people. When a child learns a word, or when I learn how a particular colleague likes to communicate, that happens through a long sequence of interactions with one other agent who has a model of me, who notices when I misunderstand, and who adjusts what they say based on what I just did.

So the question I'm interested in is, what's actually possible in that regime? If you have a single user talking to a model over days or weeks, there's a lot of information in that stream that isn't in the pretraining data. There's information about what this particular person means when they use a word idiosyncratically. There's information about what they already know, so the model doesn't have to re-explain things. And crucially, there's feedback. When the model gets something wrong, the user often tells it, implicitly or explicitly, and right now most systems just throw that signal away at the end of the context window.

From a more scientific angle, I think it's also a nice clean testbed for a question I care about a lot, which is whether these models can build and maintain something like a model of another agent. Can they infer a user's goals, their beliefs, their preferences, from a small number of observations, and then use that to make better predictions about what the user will say or want next? That's really a theory of mind question, and the single-user interaction setting is the smallest version of it where it actually matters.

And then there's a practical reason, which is that the big-corpus approach has a ceiling. There's only so much text, and a lot of what makes a system useful to a specific person just isn't written down anywhere. So I think if we want models that get better the longer you use them, in the way that a good collaborator does, we have to understand learning from interaction, and not just learning from the aggregate of everyone's interactions, but learning from yours in particular.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts interaction-based learning with large-corpus pretraining, but does not say that major industry players have limited incentives to investigate learning from smaller amounts of data.

r002.rationale: The response uses human learning as a comparison, but does not suggest that studying single-user interaction could inform how to teach people.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the remarkable things about human communication is how much we adapt to the person we’re talking to. You and I don’t need to use words in exactly the same way when we first meet. Over the course of a conversation, we can establish shared terminology, figure out what each other knows, and get better at understanding what the other person wants.

A language model trained on a huge collection of text has learned a lot about how people communicate in general. But that’s different from understanding this particular person, doing this particular task. I’m interested in how a model can close that gap through interaction: asking questions, getting corrections, and using the history it shares with a user to interpret what they say next.

That’s practically useful, because you shouldn’t have to explain everything from scratch every time you ask for help. But it’s also a scientific question about language learning. How much can you learn from a small amount of interaction when that interaction is grounded in something you’re trying to accomplish together?

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from a small amount of interaction, but says nothing about major industry players or their incentives to investigate it.

r002.rationale: It connects user interaction to human communication, but does not suggest that studying this could inform how to teach people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the interesting things about language is how much of it depends on shared context. If you and I work together for a while, I learn what you know, what you’re trying to accomplish, and what you mean when you use particular expressions. And that lets us communicate in ways that would be difficult for somebody who had just walked into the room.

Language models learn a lot from training on text from many different people. But that’s a different kind of learning from getting to know a particular person through interaction. I’m interested in what a model can learn in that setting: Can it figure out your goals? Can it learn a new concept that you introduce? Can it ask a useful question when it doesn’t understand something?

That seems important both for building useful assistants and for understanding language learning more generally. Communication isn’t just producing a plausible next sentence. It’s a process in which people build up shared knowledge and become better at working together.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts broad text training with learning from one person, but does not mention smaller data amounts or limited incentives for industry players to study that area.

r002.rationale: It says this work could help understand language learning generally, but does not suggest using it to inform how to teach people.
